I couldn't find a good sub to post this in, but it does apply to reddit and its attack on all things that hurt feelings. I wrote this for school awhile back as a troll in itself, because I really didn't like the instructor. However, I think it has become relevant for us all today.

Social Benefits of Online Deviance and Trolling

Trolling is beneficial to both to online communities and to the world outside of the internet. These benefits include online community bond strengthening, encouraging social development skills, and putting a focus on relevant issues going on in the world. The word “troll” often connotes relations to cyber bullying and online harassment, whereas they are not always mutually exclusive to each other.

The context of the definition of “troll” in the semi-classical sense is a slang-term for describing behavior on the internet that is meant to frustrate, confuse or infuriate others, most often associated with online discussions where deviant behavior is generally not welcome.

To understand the social dynamics of the impact that trolling has on a community, group, or forum, a basic understanding of social deviance is necessary. Kai T. Erikson’s view of a deviant is “considered a vagrant form of human activity, moving outside the more orderly currents of social life” (307). They are akin to a faulty wire or an anomaly to the machine of society. Deviance implies a violation or encroachment of acceptable behaviors in society. It can encompass all types of negative behavior, ranging from a seemingly harmless prank to the perpetration of cold-blooded murder. The boundaries for deviant behavior are largely dependent on the society in which the act is committed. For example, in many societies, drinking alcohol is a socially acceptable behavior, but doing so in excess can be typically be frowned upon by those around you. On the flip side, drinking in excess– even to the point of blacking out – at a college party or sporting event can be seen by others as a badge of honor. If driving is combined with alcohol consumption, then the spectrum expands outward and affects more than those in your immediate vicinity. Outside of the legal implications, local organizations exist with the sole purpose of opposition to drinking and driving, such as Mothers Against Drunk Driving and the International Drunk Driving Prevention Association. On a much broader level, drinking and driving is typically viewed as socially deviant behavior.

Trolling is a form of social deviance that typically occurs in the confines of the internet. It will take on anything on the moral spectrum, ranging from the hilarious to the obscene, and the hypocritical to the rational, and put it on display (McLemee 2011). In recent years, however, the term has been used by the mainstream media to describe any behavior that they disagree with, or see as inappropriate (Dunlop 2013). This catch-all definition of troll has trickled into the vocabulary of those who have not grown up with the internet. Often the accused is conveniently dismissed as a cyber bully, which is defined as “an aggressive act using electronic communication carried out by an individual or group of individuals directed at another person or group of people who have difficulty defending themselves” (Carter 2013).

In the context of the internet, discussion forum trolls thrive because having a deviant member of any structured group may threaten the image the group is trying to portray, as their social identities are at stake (Fortune & Newby-Clark, 2008; Marques, Paez, & Abrams, 1998). Tests results have shown that deviant behavior is especially sanctioned or disapproved by groups when a third party is introduced (Chekroun and Nugier 2011). Individuals seeking out specialized discussion groups to target can do so with ease through the use of search engines. The nature of the specific audience that discussion forums cater to creates a very rigid set of expectations and understanding within that community. The effects are two-fold. Those seeking to relate to others on certain topics and those seeking to cause disruptions can find these communities with the same ease. Trolls are drawn to such an atmosphere because of the how easily the rigid social network is broken. This notion is especially well put by the Joker in the 2008 film, The Dark Knight; “Nobody panics when things go ‘according to plan.’ Even if the plan is horrifying! If…I tell the press that…a gang banger will get shot, or a truckload of soldiers will be blown up, nobody panics, because it’s all ‘part of the plan.’ But when I say that [the] mayor will die, well then everyone loses their minds! Introduce a little anarchy. Upset the established order, and everything becomes chaos. I’m an agent of chaos” (Nolan 2008).

Trolls often demonstrate a keen sense of the hypocrisies of the world and an awareness of the general insecurities of the people who live in it. It takes someone who has their thumb on the pulse of society to be able to make another feel uncomfortable and upset over the internet, while at the same time keeping them completely unaware they are a victim in someone’s game of schadenfreude. Upon viewing someone else’s accomplishments in life, trolls can leverage this to pick apart perceived insecurities. For example, someone checks into a gym on Facebook, and perhaps takes a quick picture of the parking lot and posts about how much weight they can hold while running eight miles. However, this troll is on an entirely different route, as they were actually on their way home from Taco Bell. “This is a victimless endeavor. Those that grow upset are victims of their own self-importance and incredulity. Their looking glass self feels threatened by what might as well be its reflection” (Murphy 2013).

Trolling is not an endeavor that is limited to social deviants. Law enforcement agencies have adopted techniques used by trolls in chat rooms to pose as someone else in order to trick others into a well-orchestrated trap. An international sting operation devised to locate and arrest pedophiles who utilized the internet to prey on children was able to identify over a thousand individuals within a ten week span by trolling through social media sites and chat rooms posing as a fictional ten year old girl named “Sweetie” (Jovanovic 2013). Trolling pedophiles is not a notion specific to law enforcement, however. There was a Youtube channel called To Troll a Predator, where three men baited potential pedophiles by posing as an under-aged girl, and convinced them to meet in a public space. They were then confronted by the men who dressed themselves up as Batman or The Flash. The channel has since been shut down by Canadian law enforcement (Eördögh 2011).

Media trolls have increasingly become a focus in recent years. The Onion, a satirical news outlet, has carved for itself a niche in the national spotlight. Their use of trolling is instrumental in exposing the absurdity of some of the more extreme political and sociological viewpoints. One article entitled Planned Parenthood Opens $8 Billion Abortionplex, describes an abortion clinic that is akin to a high-end resort and spa, complete with a three-story night club and dozens of restaurants and retail outlets (The Onion 2011). This prompted Republican Congressmen John Flemming of Louisiana to alert his Facebook followers of this so-called atrocity with a link accompanying his own take on it, “More on Planned Parenthood, abortion by the wholesale” (Weinger 2012). Their reactions garnered comments expressing shock and hatred toward the government and Planned Parenthood. For those aware of the joke, it provided a clear view on how a society can become blind to common sense and judgment. The Onion’s article offered a shocking look at how easily overly-eager and ill-informed politicians (and in turn, their followers) are duped by satire. It also shines a spotlight on how these politicians readily capitalize on sensationalist manufactured media to further polarize society and advance their own political agendas.

The Daily Show is a nightly half-hour satirical news show on Comedy Central hosted by comedian Jon Stewart. Often, they air segments where the correspondents make a sport out of trolling politicians in interviews by agreeing with their most controversial topics, ushering them further until a very irrational point of view comes out. In one such example of this, correspondent Aasif Mandvi’s interview with Don Yelton, of the North Carolina GOP chair, exposed him as a bigot and a racist, where Yelton admitted that the intent behind voter ID laws was specifically to suppress democratic votes in elections. All of this was done by Mandvi pretending to agree with Yelton, trolling him along on a doomed path with leading questions during the course of their interview. As a result, Yelton was eventually fired from the North Carolina state party executive board and asked to resign from his position in Buncombe County (Millhiser 2013).

Continued in comments...
Social Benefits of Online Deviance and Trolling

....continued.

An often overlooked benefit of trolls can be likened to how an immune system interacts with a virus. The body’s T cells, over time, destroy the cells that host the infection. Once the virus has been completely removed from the body, the immune system has “acquired” the knowledge to keep that particular virus at bay (Ask a Biologist 2010). In the case of an online community forum, the virus is a troll, and the users of the forum are the T cells. They will rarely fall for the same tricks. In 2004, I witness this phenomenon firsthand. The forums for the online game World of Warcraft had a sudden explosion of people claiming that the number 1 was greater than .9999 to infinity. Those educated in mathematics promptly claimed the two were equal, but those who were trolling kept on bringing up the same dizzying logical arguments in an attempt to prove otherwise. This topic spanned an entire week, on a forum intended to focus on a completely unrelated topic to the discussion at hand. As the lengthy and heated debates ran their course, much like the common cold, anyone trying to bring up the subject 1>.9999 was promptly shut down by the community by being completely ignored. I have seen this same subject flare up on other forums as well, with the same end result. The community becomes “immune” to this specific attack, and it brings them closer together, with a certain confidence, because they’ve earned it. Much like the parent who has a child stricken with chicken pox, the parent will not catch the virus, because often it’s a battle their immune system had fought already at an early age. The benefit is that communities are strengthened by the trolls who seek to destroy them (Saccaro 2012).

Outside of the internet, deviant behavior will often take on an unintentional or well-meaning role. A new workplace rule can be put in place, but that new rule may contradict one of the more long-term policies that the company tries to promote. The worker is now forced into the role of the deviant, having to choose which policy to violate. In this case, the deviant behavior is simply a response to society’s abnormal conditions (Erikson, 307). With the case of the internet, the troll will seek these policies out and exploit them. They are acting to call out hypocrisy and useless rules, often becoming the vessel for meaningful change to a forum or website, and in the larger scale, perhaps legislation in a government.

While ignoring the neo-definitions placed on trolls in today’s media-manipulated atmosphere, trolling has created for itself a niche with positive social implications in a wide array of communities over the years. Deviant behaviors will strengthen the relationships between constructive members of a forum by having a universal “bad guy” to target, and will always become familiar with the many types of behaviors a troll may employ. The result is a solid community with a built-up immune system, able to move past social disruptions more and more efficiently over time.

Furthermore, deviant social behavior can be adapted by those looking to make a positive impact in society, looking not to stain or scar an issue, but to shine a spotlight on it, forcing the topic into the news and giving society an update on issues at the forefront. It can be beneficial to both the internet and society. A troll will target the most fertile, hot-button issues to garner the most attention possible. One person’s sport or prank quickly becomes society’s next sociological hurdle.

Keeping with popular physicists:

A Brief History of Time: From the Big Bang to Black Holes - Hawking. "Hawking attempts to explain a range of subjects in cosmology, including the big bang, black holes and light cones, to the nonspecialist reader. His main goal is to give an overview of the subject, but he also attempts to explain some complex mathematics. In the 1996 edition of the book and subsequent editions, Hawking discusses the possibility of time travel and wormholes and explores the possibility of having a universe without a quantum singularity at the beginning of time."

Cosmos - Sagan. "Cosmos has 13 chapters, corresponding to the 13 episodes of the Cosmos television series. In the original edition, each chapter is heavily illustrated. The book covers a broad range of topics, comprising Sagan's reflections on anthropological, cosmological, biological, historical, and astronomical matters from antiquity to contemporary times. Sagan reiterates his position on extraterrestrial life—that the magnitude of the universe permits the existence of thousands of alien civilizations, but no credible evidence exists to demonstrate that such life has ever visited earth.[5] Sagan explores 15 billion years of cosmic evolution and the development of science and civilization. He traces the origins of knowledge and the scientific method, mixing science and philosophy, and speculates about the future of science. He also discusses the underlying premises of science by providing biographical anecdotes about many prominent scientists, placing their contributions in the broader context of the development of modern science."

"Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman!": Adventures of a Curious Character - Fenyman. "dited collection of reminiscences by the Nobel Prize-winning physicist Richard Feynman. The book, released in 1985, covers a variety of instances in Feynman's life. Some are lighthearted in tone, such as his fascination with safe-cracking, studying various languages, participating with groups of people who share different interests (such as biology or philosophy), and ventures into art and samba music. Others cover more serious material, including his work on the Manhattan Project (during which his first wife Arline Greenbaum died of tuberculosis) and his critique of the science education system in Brazil. The section "Monster Minds" describes his slightly nervous presentation of his graduate work on the Wheeler–Feynman absorber theory in front of Albert Einstein, Wolfgang Pauli and other major figures of the time."

Death by Black Hole: And Other Cosmic Quandaries - Tyson. "Death by Black Hole is divided into seven sections: The Nature of Knowledge, The Knowledge of Nature, Ways and Means of Nature, The Meaning of Life, When the Universe Turns Bad, Science and Culture, and Science and God."

If you're a Star Trek fan, The Physics of Star Trek - Krauss. "The book discusses the physics involved in various concepts and objects described in the Star Trek universe. He investigates the possibility of such things as inertial dampeners and warp drive, and whether physics as we know it would allow such inventions. He also discusses time travel, light speed, pure energy beings, wormholes, teleportation, and other concepts that are staples of the Star Trek universe."

Biology:

The Double Helix : A Personal Account of the Discovery of the Structure of DNA - Watson. "autobiographical account of the discovery of the double helix structure of DNA written by James D. Watson and published in 1968." (editorial note: it is really important to look at this as also a primary source, mainly from letters/journals, it heavily reflects the time it was written, and the culture that surrounded it)

On the Origin of Species - Darwin. "Darwin's book introduced the scientific theory that populations evolve over the course of generations through a process of natural selection. It presented a body of evidence that the diversity of life arose by common descent through a branching pattern of evolution. Darwin included evidence that he had gathered on the Beagle expedition in the 1830s and his subsequent findings from research, correspondence, and experimentation."

(Dawkins is a popular writer, haven't read his works yet, I tend to stick to textbooks for biology).

Blend of disciplines:

Guns, Germs, and Steel: The Fates of Human Societies - Diamond. "The book attempts to explain why Eurasian civilizations (including North Africa) have survived and conquered others, while arguing against the idea that Eurasian hegemony is due to any form of Eurasian intellectual, moral, or inherent genetic superiority. Diamond argues that the gaps in power and technology between human societies originate in environmental differences, which are amplified by various positive feedback loops. When cultural or genetic differences have favored Eurasians (for example, written language or the development among Eurasians of resistance to endemic diseases), he asserts that these advantages occurred because of the influence of geography on societies and cultures, and were not inherent in the Eurasian genomes." (editorial note: Diamond places a lot of emphasis on geolocation, and as he is writing a non-fiction novel, he is more soft in his analysis, or allowing self-critique into the work)

Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid - Hofstadter. "By exploring common themes in the lives and works of logician Kurt Gödel, artist M. C. Escher and composer Johann Sebastian Bach, GEB expounds concepts fundamental to mathematics, symmetry, and intelligence. Through illustration and analysis, the book discusses how self-reference and formal rules allow systems to acquire meaning despite being made of "meaningless" elements. It also discusses what it means to communicate, how knowledge can be represented and stored, the methods and limitations of symbolic representation, and even the fundamental notion of "meaning" itself. ... Hofstadter has emphasized that GEB is not about mathematics, art, and music but rather about how cognition and thinking emerge from well-hidden neurological mechanisms. In the book, he presents an analogy about how the individual neurons of the brain coordinate to create a unified sense of a coherent mind by comparing it to the social organization displayed in a colony of ants."

Liars and Outliers: Enabling the Trust that Society Needs to Thrive - Schneier. "The book covers a wide array of disciplines, from game theory and security to sociology and evolution in its attempt to explain how trust scales from a small village in which people know and trust each other to a global economy where individuals cannot possibly trust every person they must work with, but trust the systems of law and physical security instead." (warning, reading Schneier will make you want to read more of his work, from his textbooks, other books, articles, and lean towards becoming a certain political type)

Computer Science:

Ghost in the Wires: My Adventures as the World's Most Wanted Hacker - Mitnick. "It covers his early years of hacking and social engineering and becoming a fugitive for two and a half years in the 1990's." (editorial note: companion piece to Art of Intrusion, and Art of Deception, if you're into that type of thing. just keep in mind, Mitnick writes in a way that is a natural reaction to the years of spin against him, including what ended up in Hackers 2: Operation Takedown)

The Hacker Crackdown: Law and Disorder on the Electronic Frontier - Sterling. "The book discusses watershed events in the hacker subculture in the early 1990s. The most notable topic covered is Operation Sundevil and the events surrounding the 1987-1990 war on the Legion of Doom network: the raid on Steve Jackson Games, the trial of "Knight Lightning" (one of the original journalists of Phrack), and the subsequent formation of the Electronic Frontier Foundation. The book also profiles the likes of "Emmanuel Goldstein" (publisher of 2600: The Hacker Quarterly), the former Assistant Attorney General of Arizona Gail Thackeray, FLETC instructor Carlton Fitzpatrick, Mitch Kapor, and John Perry Barlow."

ENDNOTE: Any omissions, or grievances, I apologise, I stuck to my own, personal reading. Most of the time, reading journal articles, publications, textbooks, at a certain point, you want to get back to reading fiction. I am also not going to recommend Principia Mathematica to a casual reader.
